Paper 1 is the closest: it reframes GAN training as continual learning and shows the discriminator desynchronizes from the moving generator via catastrophic forgetting, then proposes methods (momentum, EWC, gradient penalties, loss rebalancing) that reduce mode collapse. However, it never varies the G:D update ratio, never studies the D-under-updated regime, and offers no update-count synchronization schedule. Paper 4 contributes a quantitative local-stability analysis of the G:D learning-rate ratio around equilibrium, but it does not model mode collapse or a stale discriminator and gives no scheduling rule. Papers 2 and 3 attack mode collapse through other mechanisms (equilibrium memory over strategy histories, primal-dual subgradient updates) rather than D–G update synchronization, and Paper 2 concedes residual mode collapse. Thus the core canonical question — whether balanced/coordinated D and G updates prevent the Helvetica collapse — remains empirically and theoretically open, despite meaningful adjacent progress.', assessments=[PaperAssessment(paper=CandidatePaper(paper_id='arxiv_1807.04015', title='On Catastrophic Forgetting and Mode Collapse in Generative Adversarial Networks', abstract="In this paper, we show that Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) suffer from catastrophic forgetting even when they are trained to approximate a single target distribution. We show that GAN training is a continual learning problem in which the sequence of changing model distributions is the sequence of tasks to the discriminator. The level of mismatch between tasks in the sequence determines the level of forgetting. Catastrophic forgetting is interrelated to mode collapse and can make the training of GANs non-convergent. We investigate the landscape of the discriminator's output in different variants of GANs and find that when a GAN converges to a good equilibrium, real training datapoints are wide local maxima of the discriminator. We empirically show the relationship between the sharpness of local maxima and mode collapse and generalization in GANs. We show how catastrophic forgetting prevents the discriminator from making real datapoints local maxima, and thus causes non-convergence. Finally, we study methods for preventing catastrophic forgetting in GANs.", authors=['Hoang Thanh-Tung', 'Truyen Tran'], published_date='2018-07-11T09:08:34Z', url='https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.04015v8'), relevance_to_gap='partial_solution', contribution_summary="The paper attacks mode collapse and GAN non-convergence from a synchronization angle: it reframes GAN training as continual learning and shows that the discriminator catastrophically forgets previous generator distributions as the generator moves, i.e., the discriminator falls out of sync with the generator's trajectory. It then studies/designs methods that keep the discriminator aligned with the moving generator (momentum, EWC/online-EWC, R1/0GP gradient penalties, WGAN-GP, and a new imbalanced real-vs-fake loss), showing reduced mode collapse and improved convergence.", what_remains_open='The gap\'s specific mechanism — the "Helvetica scenario" of training the generator too much relative to discriminator updates, causing many z to collapse onto the single point D currently scores highest — is not investigated. SGD does not use information from previous model distributions, $p_g^{<t}$.', 'Addressing catastrophic forgetting leads to better convergence and less mode collapse.']), PaperAssessment(paper=CandidatePaper(paper_id='arxiv_1712.00679', title='GANGs: Generative Adversarial Network Games', abstract="Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) have become one of the most successful frameworks for unsupervised generative modeling. As GANs are difficult to train much research has focused on this. However, very little of this research has directly exploited game-theoretic techniques. We introduce Generative Adversarial Network Games (GANGs), which explicitly model a finite zero-sum game between a generator ($G$) and classifier ($C$) that use mixed strategies. The size of these games precludes exact solution methods, therefore we define resource-bounded best responses (RBBRs), and a resource-bounded Nash Equilibrium (RB-NE) as a pair of mixed strategies such that neither $G$ or $C$ can find a better RBBR. The RB-NE solution concept is richer than the notion of `local Nash equilibria' in that it captures not only failures of escaping local optima of gradient descent, but applies to any approximate best response computations, including methods with random restarts. To validate our approach, we solve GANGs with the Parallel Nash Memory algorithm, which provably monotonically converges to an RB-NE. We compare our results to standard GAN setups, and demonstrate that our method deals well with typical GAN problems such as mode collapse, partial mode coverage and forgetting.", authors=['Frans A. Oliehoek', 'Rahul Savani', 'Jose Gallego-Posada', 'Elise van der Pol', 'Edwin D. de Jong', 'Roderich Gross'], published_date='2017-12-02T23:38:03Z', url='https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00679v2'), relevance_to_gap='partial_solution', contribution_summary='The paper reformulates GAN training as a finite zero-sum game in mixed strategies (GANGs) and solves it with the Parallel Nash Memory algorithm, which provably and monotonically converges to a Resource-Bounded Nash Equilibrium (RB-NE). The maintained mixed strategies of generator and classifier are both recomputed and re-equilibrated each iteration, and the authors claim this "deals well with typical GAN problems such as mode collapse, partial mode coverage and forgetting," demonstrating on synthetic Gaussian-mixture domains that PNM covers modes better than standard GAN training.', what_remains_open='The gap\'s specific problem is the D–G synchronization failure mode (the "Helvetica scenario"): training G too long against a stale/fixed D lets many z collapse to one x. This paper does not analyze, measure, or manage the relative update schedule/intensity of D vs G; instead it replaces online alternated training with an equilibrium search over accumulated pure strategies of both players, keeping entire histories of classifiers (which may be deliberately \'stale\' relative to the current G) in the mixture. That is a different mechanism that sidesteps rather than directly solves the synchronization problem. Moreover, the paper concedes that mode collapse is not fully eliminated even by its method ("some amount of mode collapse still takes place") and that reducing G\'s learning rate — i.e., slowing G relative to C, an implicit synchronization tweak borrowed from WGAN — was needed to mitigate it; and experiments are restricted to low-dimensional synthetic Gaussian mixtures, with no direct investigation of the Helvetica/collapse-to-a-point dynamics.', evidence_snippets=['We investigate empirically the effectiveness of PNM and show that it can indeed deal well with typical GAN problems such as mode collapse, partial mode coverage and forgetting, especially in distributions with less symmetric structure to their modes.', "As also pointed out by, e.g.,~[CITE:ACB17_WGAN], the best response of $G$ against $\\mA C$ is a single point with the highest `realness', and therefore the WGAN they introduced uses fewer iterations for $G$ than for $C$. Inspired by this, we investigate if we can reduce the mode collapse by reducing the learning rate of $G$ (to $10^{-5}$).", 'The above results show that PNM can accurately cover multiple modes, however, not all modes are fully covered; some amount of mode collapse still takes place.']), PaperAssessment(paper=CandidatePaper(paper_id='arxiv_1802.01765', title='Training Generative Adversarial Networks via Primal-Dual Subgradient Methods: A Lagrangian Perspective on GAN', abstract='We relate the minimax game of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to finding the saddle points of the Lagrangian function for a convex optimization problem, where the discriminator outputs and the distribution of generator outputs play the roles of primal variables and dual variables, respectively. This formulation shows the connection between the standard GAN training process and the primal-dual subgradient methods for convex optimization. The inherent connection does not only provide a theoretical convergence proof for training GANs in the function space, but also inspires a novel objective function for training. The modified objective function forces the distribution of generator outputs to be updated along the direction according to the primal-dual subgradient methods. A toy example shows that the proposed method is able to resolve mode collapse, which in this case cannot be avoided by the standard GAN or Wasserstein GAN. Experiments on both Gaussian mixture synthetic data and real-world image datasets demonstrate the performance of the proposed method on generating diverse samples.', authors=['Xu Chen', 'Jiang Wang', 'Hao Ge'], published_date='2018-02-06T02:31:43Z', url='https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01765v1'), relevance_to_gap='partial_solution', contribution_summary='The paper reformulates GAN training as primal-dual subgradient methods for a convex optimization (discriminator outputs = primal variables, generator output probabilities = dual variables), proves that updating D and p_g according to the primal-dual rules converges to the saddle point (p_g -> p_d) in function space, and proposes a modified generator loss that pushes p_g toward the "optimal update direction" from the dual subgradient rule. This is designed to avoid mode collapse even when the discriminator is saturated/stuck (their toy example), and experiments on mixture-of-Gaussians, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 report improved diversity.', what_remains_open='The gap\'s specific problem is the *synchronization* between D and G during training — i.e., training G too many steps without updating D (the "Helvetica scenario"). The paper does not address this update-balance/scheduling problem. It never considers the ratio of discriminator to generator inner-loop updates or the regime where G is updated repeatedly against a stale D; its theory assumes the ideal primal-dual rules with a suitable step size in function space, and its modified generator loss works by decoupling the generator update from the discriminator\'s gradient (via a kernel density estimate of p_g) rather than by keeping D synchronized with G. The toy example involves a discriminator that has already reached its local optimum (zero gradient) rather than a D that lags behind G. Moreover, the convergence guarantee relies on convexity in the function space, kernel density estimation that suffers the curse of dimensionality, and only covers the added regularization term; the central question of how to schedule D and G updates to keep them synchronized is left open.', evidence_snippets=['The update of the discriminator is the same as standard GAN training. The main difference is the modified loss function for the generator update~[REF:eq:update_gen]. The intuition is that when the generated samples have disjoint support from the data, the generated distribution at the data support may not be updated using standard training. This is exactly one source of mode collapse.', 'In our proposed training method, when $x=1$, the optimal update direction is given by~[REF:eq:update_pg], where $\\tilde{p}_g$ is a large value because $D(1) = 1$. Therefore, by [REF:eq:update_gen], the second term in the loss function is very large, which forces the generator to generate samples at $G(\\bz) = 1$.', 'The primal-dual update rules will guarantee convergence of $\\left( \\bD^{(t)}, \\bp_g^{(t)} \\right)$ to the primal-dual saddle point ($\\bD^{\\ast},\\bp^{\\ast}_g$).']), PaperAssessment(paper=CandidatePaper(paper_id='arxiv_2305.08277', title='Local Convergence of Gradient Descent-Ascent for Training Generative Adversarial Networks', abstract='Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a popular formulation to train generative models for complex high dimensional data. The standard method for training GANs involves a gradient descent-ascent (GDA) procedure on a minimax optimization problem. This procedure is hard to analyze in general due to the nonlinear nature of the dynamics. We study the local dynamics of GDA for training a GAN with a kernel-based discriminator. This convergence analysis is based on a linearization of a non-linear dynamical system that describes the GDA iterations, under an \\textit{isolated points model} assumption from [Becker et al. 2022]. Our analysis brings out the effect of the learning rates, regularization, and the bandwidth of the kernel discriminator, on the local convergence rate of GDA. Importantly, we show phase transitions that indicate when the system converges, oscillates, or diverges. We also provide numerical simulations that verify our claims.', authors=['Evan Becker', 'Parthe Pandit', 'Sundeep Rangan', 'Alyson K. Fletcher'], published_date='2023-05-14T23:23:08Z', url='https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.08277v2'), relevance_to_gap='partial_solution', contribution_summary='The paper analyzes the coupled generator/discriminator GDA dynamics for a kernel-based (RBF/MMD) discriminator GAN under an isolated-points model. It linearizes the joint update map around the equilibrium where generated points sit on true points and derives an exact eigenvalue characterization in terms of the generator and discriminator learning rates (and their ratio μ), regularization λ, and kernel width σ, giving necessary/sufficient conditions for local stability, convergence-rate bounds, and phase transitions between convergence, oscillation, and divergence. This bears on the synchronization problem by quantifying how mismatched generator-vs-discriminator learning (e.g., too-large η_g relative to η_d and kernel capacity) destabilizes training.', what_remains_open="The gap's core problem is mode collapse / the 'Helvetica scenario': if G is trained too much without D being kept synchronized, many z values collapse to the same x and diversity is lost. The paper does not analyze this scenario: its local analysis is confined to neighborhoods of an equilibrium where generated points already match the true points, under strong assumptions (isolated points, RBF kernel with zero cross-region interaction, equal generated masses), and it studies whether points converge to the true samples, not whether the generator's latent diversity collapses into a single mode or which z-values map to the same output. It never models an over-trained generator versus a stale/under-trained discriminator, and it provides no synchronization scheduling rule (e.g., number/ratio of D updates per G update) to prevent mode collapse. Its contribution is instead stability and convergence-rate conditions for simultaneous GDA around an equilibrium, which is only tangentially related to keeping D synchronized to avoid diversity collapse.", evidence_snippets=['Our analysis brings out the effect of the learning rates, regularization, and the bandwidth of the kernel discriminator, on the local convergence rate of GDA. Importantly, we show phase transitions that indicate when the system converges, oscillates, or diverges.', 'In practice, however, we apply GDA for training GANs, whereby the discriminator is not allowed to converge, making analysis of the iterative training extremely difficult. Furthermore, training commonly suffers from empirical breakdowns such as mode collapse, in which the entire generated distribution converges to a small portion of the target distribution', 'The training dynamics [REF:eq:gda_local] are stable around equilibrium $\\wt\\X_i^*$ from [REF:eq:xeq] for all $\\Delta_i \\in (0,p_i)$ if, ... $\\eta_d < \\frac2\\lambda$, and $\\eta_g<\\lambda\\sigma^2$.']), PaperAssessment(paper=CandidatePaper(paper_id='arxiv_1802.06132', title='Interaction Matters: A Note on Non-asymptotic Local Convergence of Generative Adversarial Networks', abstract='Motivated by the pursuit of a systematic computational and algorithmic understanding of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), we present a simple yet unified non-asymptotic local convergence theory for smooth two-player games, which subsumes several discrete-time gradient-based saddle point dynamics. The analysis reveals the surprising nature of the off-diagonal interaction term as both a blessing and a curse. On the one hand, this interaction term explains the origin of the slow-down effect in the convergence of Simultaneous Gradient Ascent (SGA) to stable Nash equilibria. On the other hand, for the unstable equilibria, exponential convergence can be proved thanks to the interaction term, for four modified dynamics proposed to stabilize GAN training: Optimistic Mirror Descent (OMD), Consensus Optimization (CO), Implicit Updates (IU) and Predictive Method (PM). The analysis uncovers the intimate connections among these stabilizing techniques, and provides detailed characterization on the choice of learning rate. As a by-product, we present a new analysis for OMD proposed in Daskalakis, Ilyas, Syrgkanis, and Zeng [2017] with improved rates.', authors=['Tengyuan Liang', 'James Stokes'], published_date='2018-02-16T21:30:19Z', url='https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.06132v2'), relevance_to_gap='not_addressed', contribution_summary='The paper develops a non-asymptotic local convergence theory for discrete-time gradient-based dynamics (SGA, OMD, Consensus Optimization, Implicit Updates, Predictive Methods) on smooth two-player zero-sum games of GAN form. It characterizes exponential convergence to stable local Nash equilibria for SGA and exponential convergence to unstable (bi-linear) equilibria for the four modified dynamics, framing the off-diagonal interaction term as both a curse and a blessing for convergence rates. These results concern which update *dynamics* converge and at what rate, under the assumption that both players are updated simultaneously (once per iteration).', what_remains_open='The gap\'s specific problem is that the discriminator and generator must remain synchronized in update frequency — training G too much without updating D causes the "Helvetica scenario" in which many z collapse to the same x (mode collapse). This paper never studies imbalanced/asymmetric update schedules between the two players: all analyzed dynamics (SGA, OMD, CO, IU, PM) and all experiments update generator and discriminator together once per iteration. It does not analyze regimes where one player is updated more often than the other, does not discuss the k-D-steps-per-G-step rule, and does not connect unequal update rates to diversity loss/mode collapse or the Helvetica scenario. Its scope is instead local convergence rates of equal-rate simultaneous dynamics toward local Nash equilibria, so the synchronization problem motivating the gap remains open.', evidence_snippets=['The simplest possibility is Simultaneous Gradient Ascent (SGA), which corresponds to the following discrete-time dynamical system, ...', 'In this section we will establish the non-asymptotic convergence of SGA dynamics to saddle points that are stable local Nash equilibria.', 'we optimize the above loss functions using simultaneous gradient updates with fixed learning rate of $\\eta = 10^{-3}$.'])], metadata={'queries_used': ['literal', 'reframed', 'broad'], 'candidate_count': 15, 'papers_deep_read': 5, 'skipped_ids': []}), ranking=RankingScores(openness=0.3, impact=0.3990274132982, feasibility=0.8, feasibility_reasoning='This is a focused, empirically testable extension of existing GAN work. The needed data is cheap and standard (toy Gaussian mixtures for controlled mode-collapse measurement, plus MNIST/CIFAR if desired), and compute is modest — varying the G:D update ratio requires only small-scale GAN training runs on a single GPU. The methodological path is a direct extension of known training loops: sweep update-count/learning-rate ratios, intentionally stale the discriminator, and measure mode collapse with established diversity metrics (number of recovered modes, precision/recall, FID). The main feasibility risks are GAN training variance and the need for careful seeds/repeats, but these are manageable engineering concerns, not fundamental barriers; a clear empirical answer (and possibly a simple scheduling rule) is achievable.'))] ideas=[IdeaRecord(idea_id='idea_b7e9ecbe', title='Cascade ratio control: a PI supervisor that closes the D–G synchronization loop with anti-windup', state='root', one_liner="GANs today set the G-to-D update ratio open-loop (TTUR fixes it); I import cascade ratio control from process control to close that loop — a slow PI supervisor measures D's tracking residual and continuously retunes how many D steps run per G step, with anti-windup for the saturated discriminator regime.", description='The Helvetica collapse is an open-loop ratio failure: we hand-set how many D updates run per G update and never verify, mid-run, that D actually still tracks the moving generator. In cascade/ratio control, two loops whose plant drifts are never coupled open-loop — an outer controller senses a measured variable and retunes the inner-loop setpoint, with anti-windup for when the inner actuator saturates. Transfer: the inner loop is standard alternating D updates (the fast loop that must track the current p_g); the "sensor" is D itself; the measured controlled variable is D\'s online tracking residual (how well D still separates real from current fakes at a modest, bounded edge); the manipulated variable is the D/G update ratio and the G step size; and the outer PI controller nulls the steady-state residual error while a rate limiter and anti-windup clamp it when D saturates to a perfect classifier. This is cheap (only scalar statistics from the D batches), reactive rather than predictive (unlike unrolled GANs\' K-step lookahead), and closes the loop TTUR leaves open.', problem="Synchronization of D with a moving G is currently enforced by a fixed, hand-chosen training ratio, which drifts out of validity whenever G's dynamics change regime — and that drift is exactly when many z collapse to one x. The idea targets the open-loop nature of ratio scheduling: sense when D has lost track of G and adapt the ratio in closed loop, rather than guessing a ratio that holds for all phases of training.", addresses=['gap_f19d02aa'], relations=[], inherited_from=None, sections={'technique': "Treat (G, D) as a cascade plant. Inner loop: standard D updates tracking the current G. Outer loop (per K G-steps, e.g. K=50):\n\n1. Measure residual r_t from the discriminator's own batch statistics — a scalar that grows when D is stale. Candidate: signed difference between D's mean logit on real vs fake batches, kept inside a target band near a small edge (not 0, so G keeps a gradient; not large, so D doesn't saturate), combined with the cross-z variance of D(G(z)) to catch collapse (spiked near-zero variance = many z on one x).\n2. PI update u_t = clamp(u_{t-1} + Kp*e_t + Ki*sum(e), [u_min, u_max], rate_limit), e_t = target − r_t, where u_t is the D-steps-per-G-step ratio.\n3. Anti-windup: when D is saturated (its real-vs-fake edge pegged at max), freeze the integrator and/or force G steps — a saturated D is no longer a valid sensor and its accumulated error must not overdrive the controller.\n4. Optionally the same loop also scales G's step size (manipulate the disturbance entering the inner loop directly).\nAll quantities are running means of scalar discriminator outputs; no architectural change, no extra networks, no unrolling.", 'term_by_term_transfer': '- Plant = the coupled (G, D) system; the "disturbance" into the D loop is G\'s movement.\n- Sensor / measurement = D itself, read only near its current operating point (a stale D is an out-of-bandwidth sensor, which is precisely the control-theoretic name for the Helvetica failure).\n- Inner (secondary) loop = fast alternating D updates that must track moving p_g; its bandwidth must exceed the rate G changes.\n- Outer (primary) controller = slow PI supervisor, updated every K steps, whose output is the inner-loop ratio setpoint.\n- Anti-windup = the fix for the known regime where D becomes a perfect classifier and its feedback saturates.\n- Rate limiter / integrator clamping = boundedness guarantee that no single regime change spikes the ratio.\nWhere the analogy breaks: G and D have no clean state-space model, so the controller gains must be tuned online or scheduled rather than derived; and r_t is a stochastic proxy, so the controller needs noise filtering at timescales longer than a batch.', 'known_and_what_it_adds': "Known and not re-proposed: TTUR (Heusel 2017) fixes two separate learning rates open-loop — it never measures whether D actually tracks G. Unrolled GANs (Metz 2017) *predict* D's next step with a K-step unroll, a forward-model solution that is expensive and gives G an anticipatory gradient rather than supervising the ratio. Spectral norm / gradient penalties stabilize D's landscape but don't address the pacing of G vs D.\n\nWhat this adds: the ratio becomes a feedback signal driven by a measured desynchronization residual instead of a constant; the controller nulls steady-state error (so the residual self-corrects rather than diverging across regimes); and the anti-windup + rate-limiter machinery is the concrete mechanism no listed prior work carries. Reactive and near-free compared with unrolling. (Claimed absence of a closed-loop supervisory ratio in prior GAN work is unverified — there are adaptive-ratio heuristics in the DCGAN/StyleGAN folklore, but to my knowledge none framed or stabilized as a PI controller with anti-windup.)", 'assumptions_and_limits': "- There exists an online scalar statistic that cleanly separates 'desynchronized' from 'well-synced but diverse' from 'collapsed' — near-1/2 discriminator output is ambiguous across the last two, so the residual may need the cross-z variance term or a two-metric controller (open question).\n- Controller gains must be scheduled or auto-tuned since the plant is nonlinear and unmodeled; wrong Kp/Ki can itself oscillate the ratio.\n- The scheme assumes D-batch statistics are cheap and stably estimable, i.e., batch sizes and K are large enough that r_t is not dominated by noise.\n- It does not by itself stop collapse within a single G burst; it is a supervisory layer that must act before G runs far ahead, so K (outer-loop period) must be short enough relative to G's drift rate.", 'open_questions': '- Which online statistic best isolates desync without confounding good convergence with collapse? Does the cross-z variance of D(G(z)) track the Helvetica precursor early enough to act?\n- Direction and scheduling of the PI action across regimes: when D is *too* good the fix is fewer D steps, but when G is racing ahead the fix is more D steps — can one controller sign handle both, or is this two-mode gain scheduling?\n- Interaction with existing stabilizers (spectral norm, penalty terms): does closing the ratio loop make them redundant, or compose?\n- Order-of-magnitude of K, Kp, Ki, and the ratio band for a controlled test on a toy multimodal Gaussian before any image benchmark.', 'rationale': "Stance: transferer. The abstract problem — two coupled loops whose plant drifts and whose sensor saturates — is not a GAN problem; it is the textbook problem cascade/ratio control with anti-windup was built to solve, and the term-by-term mapping above is exact enough to import, not just borrow words from, control engineering. This is deliberately distinct from the optimizer angle (which would improve the loss/updates) and the skeptic angle (which would make G robust to stale D): here the fix is a control loop on the update cadence.\n\nUnverified claims: (1) that no published GAN method closes this ratio loop with measured-feedback PI control plus anti-windup — I cannot confirm this from memory and it is the key novelty risk; (2) that an online residual based on D's real-vs-fake edge and cross-z variance is a clean desync statistic — this is the empirical crux of the idea. Both are flagged as open."}, section_order=['technique', 'term_by_term_transfer', 'known_and_what_it_adds', 'assumptions_and_limits', 'open_questions', 'rationale'], evaluation=Evaluation(novelty=None, feasibility=None, significance=None), provenance=[], origin=IdeaOrigin(run_id='run_046672c3', node_id='run_046672c3:n1', node_path=['run_046672c3:n0', 'run_046672c3:n1'], style='transferer', mode='generation', parent_idea_id=None, suggested=None, inherited_from=None, inherited_upto_run=None), runs=[RunEntry(run_id='run_046672c3', session_id='sess_54885cfa', timestamp='2026-09-09T14:05:44Z', header=RunHeader(mode='generation', width=3, depth=1, model='reasoner', agent_styles=['transferer', 'skeptic', 'optimizer'], context_ids=['gap_f19d02aa', 'arxiv_1406.2661'], triggering_action='', tool_use=True, task="The gap: in GAN training the discriminator must stay synchronized with the generator. Training G too far ahead of D produces the 'Helvetica scenario' — many z values collapse to the same x and the model loses diversity.
